Season-level gains with the observed ONI vary widely (SD 0.134 over 20 seasons); the two largest in absolute value, 2024 (+0.457) and 2020 (−0.311), account for most of that spread (87% of the squared deviations from the mean) rather than the mean, which is +0.038 without them. display: In this synthesis of El Niño and health in India, no ENSO index was clearly preferred over the traditional ONI (pooled leave-one-El-Niño-out prediction error across 3 outcomes). For malaria, the ENSO-attributable out-of-sample log-score gain (observed ONI over a climatological ENSO value; positive = better) was −0.010 nats per unit-year (95% CI −0.020 to +0.001), not clearly different from zero. The observed-ONI model's gain over the no-ENSO comparison model (local climate, trend and programme terms and the lagged outcome) was −0.017 nats per unit-year (95% CI −0.041 to +0.007). For recorded heat deaths, the ENSO-attributable out-of-sample log-score gain was −0.002 nats per unit-year (95% CI −0.015 to +0.011), not clearly different from zero. The observed-ONI model's gain of +0.042 nats per unit-year (95% CI −0.021 to +0.104) over the no-ENSO comparison model is consistent with the non-ENSO Indian Ocean Dipole term that the model with ENSO terms also adds. State ranks on the El Niño Health Risk Index had a median 95% rank interval of 9 places across 32 ranked units and were broadly stable across weighting schemes (minimum Kendall τ 0.80).
